title: Circuits and Ohm's Law
hook: Three quantities run every circuit — voltage, current, and resistance — and one tidy rule ties them together: voltage equals current times resistance.
key_points: Voltage is the push, current is the flow of charge, resistance is the opposition.
Ohm's law: V = I × R links all three in one relationship.
More voltage drives more current; more resistance throttles the current.
Water analogy: voltage is pressure, current is flow rate, resistance is a narrow pipe.
content_html: Almost everything you need to reason about a simple circuit comes down to three quantities. Voltage is the push that drives charge around; current is how much charge actually flows; and resistance is how strongly the circuit fights that flow. Ohm's law states the relationship between them in one line: voltage equals current times resistance, V = I × R.
extra_html: The rule is intuitive once you picture water in a pipe. Voltage is the water pressure, current is the flow rate, and resistance is a narrowing of the pipe. Crank up the pressure and more water flows; pinch the pipe and the flow drops. So raising voltage increases current, while raising resistance throttles it back. That single equation lets you predict how a circuit behaves and is the starting point for designing nearly any electronic device. Wikipedia covers the law and its limits.

flashcards.back_html: Voltage = current × resistance (V = I × R). It ties together the push, the flow, and the opposition in a circuit.

flashcards.prompt: If you increase the resistance in a circuit while voltage stays the same, the current...
flashcards.explanation_html: From V = I × R, holding voltage fixed and raising resistance forces the current down — more opposition means less flow.

flashcards.prompt: In the water-pipe analogy, what plays the role of voltage?

choices.text: The flow rate of the water

flashcards.explanation_html: Voltage is the pressure that pushes charge; current is the flow rate and resistance is how narrow the pipe is.
